design_detail: Nature Reviews Disease Primers Primer on cannabis use and cannabis use disorder (CUD), read as the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (published version: Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7:16). Six authors from the University of Queensland, the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and University of Toronto, LMU Munich and Dartmouth, each section written by named authors (Author contributions). Sections: epidemiology; mechanisms and pathophysiology (endocannabinoid system, reward, brain alterations, genetics, learning processes, risk and protective factors, a proposed multifactorial model); diagnosis, screening and prevention (DSM-5 and ICD-11 criteria, withdrawal, assessment tools, differential diagnosis, prevention, lower-risk use guidelines); management (withdrawal, psychosocial treatment, pharmacotherapy); quality of life; outlook. 326 references, three tables, four boxes and six figures (images; legends read). No search strategy, selection criteria or appraisal method; the effectiveness and confidence ratings in Table 2 are taken from systematic reviews (refs 155, 210, 215). Products with CBD and little or no THC are outside the scope.
can_establish: How six CUD researchers summarized, in 2021, the epidemiology, diagnostic criteria, mechanisms and treatment of cannabis use disorder, and which sources they cite for each figure; it can be cited for the DSM-5 and ICD-11 definitions it tabulates and as a pointer to primary studies and systematic reviews.
cannot_establish: A single risk of developing CUD (its figures use different definitions, diagnostic systems, time frames and denominators and are not reconciled), whether cannabis causes psychosis, cognitive impairment or other outcomes, treatment effects beyond those of the systematic reviews it cites, or the completeness of the evidence (no systematic search).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The evidence was chosen by the authors; no databases, dates or criteria are given.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated. Cannabis is defined as plant material or extracts with substantial THC; CBD products with no or very little THC are not reviewed (Introduction (unheaded), 2nd and 5th paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Not applicable. Cited data come mainly from US surveys (NESARC, NESARC-III, NSDUH, Monitoring the Future), Australian national mental-health surveys, Washington State, the Netherlands and Denmark, and global estimates (UN World Drug Report 2020; Global Burden of Disease 2016).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors'. 47 of the 326 references list at least one of the Primer's authors among their printed names (editors' count; lists shortened to et al. may hide more), including the two Cochrane reviews on which the treatment sections rest (refs 155 and 225, both with Le Foll), the WHO report cited for most health effects (ref 10, Hall) and one of the two reviews cited for 30–40% dependence with daily use (ref 15, Budney). Several key epidemiological figures come from reports and reviews rather than primary studies (refs 1, 10, 15, 31).

exposure.measurement: Varies by cited source: ever use, past-year use, weekly or daily use, age at first use, and potency of products. The Primer states that epidemiological research usually measures only frequency of use and lacks adequate measures of the amount of THC consumed, and that a standard THC unit has been recommended (refs 252, 253) (Outlook › Cannabis consumption measures, 1st paragraph). Box 3 lists what a clinical assessment covers (frequency, quantity, THC to CBD ratio where possible, usual pattern, mode of use, duration).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not quantified beyond frequency categories (weekly, daily or near daily); US adults with CUD are said to use on 6.2 of 10 days on average over a year (ref 44).
exposure.polysubstance: Described as the norm: 83.5% of men and 82.9% of women with past-year CUD had another substance use disorder (ref 54); three in four people in CUD treatment are said to have another (cited to DSM-5, ref 4); co-use with tobacco goes with more CUD, more withdrawal symptoms and less cessation (ref 46). Other substance use is not treated as a confounder of the associations reported, beyond any adjustment in the cited studies.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not stated for most cited studies. Cognitive recovery studies are said rarely to follow people beyond 4 weeks (ref 121), and CB1 receptor density to normalize within a few days to 4 weeks of abstinence (refs 94, 98).

comparison.controls: Varies: people who use cannabis without CUD and people who do not use it (comorbidity), controls in imaging studies, non-active treatment, waiting list, psychological placebo or treatment as usual (psychosocial trials), placebo (pharmacotherapy trials).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The Primer names shared genetic and environmental liability for early onset (Epidemiology › Age of onset), for other drug use (Box 2) and for psychosis (Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Differential diagnosis, 2nd paragraph), and says it is unclear whether dopamine-system differences reflect vulnerability or neuroadaptation (Mechanisms/pathophysiology › Brain alterations, 2nd paragraph). Pre-use baselines are not discussed for the cognitive evidence.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed for the cited studies.

outcomes.instruments: DSM-IV-TR and DSM-5 CUD, ICD-11 hazardous use, harmful pattern of use and dependence (Table 1); DSM-5 cannabis withdrawal; assessment tools such as Timeline Follow-Back, the Severity of Dependence Scale and the CIDI (Box 3); PET measures of CB1 receptors, FAAH and the dopamine system; functional and structural MRI; cognitive test batteries as pooled in meta-analyses; quality-of-life scales; frequency of use, abstinence and urinary THC-COOH in trials.
outcomes.validity_norms: As cited: the Severity of Dependence Scale distinguished people who used regularly with and without DSM-III-R dependence with sensitivity 64% and specificity 82% (ref 183); Timeline Follow-Back agreed with biological markers about 90% of the time (ref 184).
outcomes.operationalization: DSM-5 CUD requires 2 of 11 criteria with marked impairment or distress within 12 months (mild 2–3, moderate 4–5, severe 6 or more); ICD-11 dependence can be diagnosed after 1 month if use is daily or almost daily. Older cited figures use DSM-III-R or DSM-IV dependence (or DSM-IV abuse), which are not equivalent to DSM-5 CUD.

analysis.effect_sizes: All second-hand; no pooling. Use and burden: 192 million people (3.9% of adults) used in the past year in 2018, 9.9% of them daily or near daily (ref 1); 22.1 million people met CUD criteria in 2016, 289.7 per 100,000 (ref 6). Risk of dependence or CUD: about 10% of people who use (abstract); about 1 in 10 people who use regularly and up to one-third of people who use daily (ref 1); 9% lifetime dependence among people who had ever tried cannabis in a 1992 estimate, against 32% for tobacco, 23% heroin, 17% cocaine and 15% alcohol (ref 30); 30–40% with a history of daily use (refs 15, 31); about 30% of people who use in recent US national data (ref 32); 17.0% of people who smoke weekly and 19.0% of those who smoke daily met dependence criteria, and 9.7% of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (ref 45). Withdrawal: 12% of people who use frequently had DSM-5 withdrawal in the past 12 months (ref 177); 12–17% of people who use in the general population; 54% of outpatients and 87% of inpatients with CUD seeking treatment report clinically severe withdrawal (refs 177, 203). Comorbidity: another psychiatric disorder in 7 in 10 people with CUD, 4 in 10 people who use without CUD and 1.5 in 10 people who do not use (ref 47); odds ratios for past-year CUD with any mood disorder 3.8, anxiety disorder 2.8, PTSD 4.3 and personality disorder 4.8, and, adjusted, with alcohol use disorder 6.0 and any other drug use disorder 9.0 (ref 44). Treatment: Hedges g 0.44 for psychosocial treatment against control conditions at 2–14 weeks (ref 210); combined MET and CBT reduced frequency of use by 25% and doubled abstinence at a median of 4 months (ref 155); cannabis-specific prevention programmes median Cohen's d 0.12 against 0.30 for general drug-prevention programmes (ref 196). Genetics: twin heritability 40% (women) and 48% (men) for starting use and 59% and 51% for use with abuse or dependence symptoms (ref 43); 11% of the variance in lifetime use from common variants (ref 129).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable. The odds ratios of 6.0 and 9.0 are stated as adjusted for sex, race and sociodemographic and other variables; adjustment is not described for the other estimates.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The dependence figures are listed side by side without their definitions or any reconciliation. The Mendelian randomization result of the genome-wide study cited for genetics (ref 129, whose reference annotation says it tests the direction of causality between cannabis use and schizophrenia) is not reported in the text. The body's mostly null trend data (stable adult CUD prevalence 2002–2014; no rise in youth use 2010–2016 in the study cited; no overall rise in school-age prevalence 2017–2019, alongside more frequent use among adults who use and more daily use and vaping among school-age youth) do not appear in the abstract, which says legalization may increase CUD.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As cited, the risk of meeting criteria for cannabis dependence or CUD is about 1 in 10 on the older lifetime-dependence measure among people who ever used, and higher on newer or frequency-restricted measures (17–19% of people smoking weekly or daily; 30–40% of people with daily use; about 30% of people who use, in recent US data). CUD co-occurs with other psychiatric and substance use disorders; psychosocial treatment has moderate short-term effects with few gains maintained beyond 9 months; no medication is approved.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract gives about 10% of 193 million people who use worldwide, while the introduction gives 192 million and 1 in 10 people who use regularly, and the epidemiology section about 30% of people who use; the authors suggest, without data, that the higher recent figure reflects increased potency, legal change and acceptance. The abstract says psychosocial treatments can substantially reduce use and problems, where the body reports a moderate pooled effect (g 0.44 at 2–14 weeks), a 25% reduction in frequency at a median of 4 months and few gains maintained beyond 9 months; the abstract does add that enduring abstinence is uncommon. The suggestion, drawn from a monozygotic co-twin comparison, that "the adverse cognitive effects of cannabis may be reversed by sustained abstinence" rests on a study whose title says it measured self-reported health, socio-demographics and quality of life, not cognition (ref 233; Quality of life, 3rd paragraph). The expectation that commercial legalization will raise CUD rests on the analogy with alcohol and is hedged in the abstract, while the body's trend data are mostly null.

timeline.event: US National Comorbidity Survey, the source of the Primer's 9% lifetime dependence among people who had ever used (9.1%, DSM-III-R; card sc_anthony_1994).

Monozygotic co-twin comparison of residual effects on self-reported health, socio-demographics and quality of life in men (Eisen et al., 2002), cited as suggesting that cognitive effects may reverse with sustained abstinence.

Gateway tests cited: in Box 2, modelling showing that shared risk factors can explain the associations with other illicit drugs (Morral et al., 2002) and a discordant-twin study in which the twin who used cannabis is described as marginally more likely to use other drugs (Lynskey et al., 2003); in the main text, a birth cohort followed for up to 25 years (Fergusson et al., 2006, ref 58).
Recent US national data cited for about 30% of people who use developing CUD (Hasin et al., 2015); the measure and denominator are not stated in the Primer.
Critical overview cited for the view that the causal case for psychosis is contested because of shared genetic and environmental liability (card sc_ksir_2016).
Systematic review cited for some cognitive improvement after sustained abstinence, mainly in learning and memory, with follow-up rarely beyond 4 weeks (card sc_broyd_2016).

Cochrane review of psychosocial interventions (Gates et al., 2016; Le Foll a co-author), one of the three sources of the effectiveness ratings in Table 2 and of the 25% reduction in frequency; the Cochrane review of pharmacotherapies (Nielsen et al., 2019; Le Foll a co-author) is the first source cited on medications.
Re-analysis of crash studies, cited for a small contribution of cannabis use to motor vehicle crashes (card sc_rogeberg_2016).
National Academies report, cited for the lack of evidence of therapeutic benefit for most conditions for which medical use has been approved (card sc_nasem_2017).

Genome-wide association study of lifetime use (Pasman et al., 2018), cited for 11% of the variance; its Mendelian randomization result, stronger from liability to schizophrenia to cannabis use than the reverse (card sc_pasman_2018), is not reported in the text.
EU-GEI multicentre case–control study (Di Forti et al., 2019), cited for the concern that high-potency cannabis may raise the risk of psychotic disorders (card sc_di_forti_2019).
Meta-analysis of withdrawal prevalence (Bahji et al., 2020), cited for the general-population and treatment-sample figures; read in this round.
Systematic review and meta-analysis of CUD among people who use cannabis, not cited in this Primer: pooled CUD 22% (18 to 26) and dependence 13% (10 to 15) (card sc_leung_2020).

replication.where_it_stands: A 2021 overview of CUD written by clinical and epidemiological researchers in the field. Its definitions (Table 1) are standard; its epidemiological figures are second-hand and on different measures, and the meta-analytic estimate published shortly before it (Leung et al., 2020) is not cited. For how many people who use cannabis develop dependence or CUD, claims should cite the primary surveys and Leung et al. (2020), stating each time the diagnostic system, the time frame and the denominator; the Primer is best cited for diagnostic criteria and as a pointer.

funding.funder: As printed in the Acknowledgements: the Australian National Centre for Youth Substance Use Research (Connor, Hall, Stjepanović) is funded by the Australian Government under the Commonwealth Drug and Alcohol Program grant; Le Foll is supported by a clinician-scientist award from the Department of Family and Community Medicine, University of Toronto, and by the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health; Hoch has received research grants from the German Federal Ministry of Health and the European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction; Budney is supported in part by NIDA grants P30DA029926, T32DA037202 and R01DA050032. The funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed under Competing interests: Le Foll has had funding from Pfizer (GRAND Awards, including salary support) for investigator-initiated projects; in-kind donation of cannabis product from Aurora; medication donations from Pfizer and Bioprojet; a TMS coil from Brainsway; industry funding from Canopy (research grants handled by CAMH or the University of Toronto), Bioprojet, ACS and Alkermes; and in-kind donations of nabiximols from GW Pharma for past studies funded by CIHR and NIH. Hoch receives fees for trainings on CUD treatment from clinics and public-health organizations and royalties from Hogrefe Publishing for a CUD treatment manual. All other authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: By the Author contributions, Le Foll, who declares the industry ties above, co-wrote the Management and Outlook sections, which summarize pharmacotherapy (Table 3) including nabiximols, a product he declares receiving in kind; Hoch, who receives royalties for a treatment manual, co-wrote the diagnosis, screening and prevention section and the Outlook. Le Foll is also an author of several of the reviews on which the treatment sections rest (refs 155, 178, 209, 216, 225). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the Primer.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts of people who start using cannabis, with repeated DSM-5 assessments and measured THC exposure (standard units, product potency), reporting the cumulative probability of incident CUD by frequency, age of onset and product type in legal and illegal markets; for treatment, adequately powered trials with follow-up beyond 9 months.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the authors chose the evidence, section by section.

No formal appraisal; Table 2 borrows effectiveness and confidence ratings from systematic reviews without saying how they were graded, and epidemiological figures are given without their definitions. Limitations are named for some bodies of evidence (weak prevention studies, few and poor pharmacotherapy trials, cognitive follow-up rarely beyond 4 weeks, small imaging samples).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 47 of 326 references include an author of the Primer, among them the two Cochrane reviews behind the treatment sections and the WHO report cited for most health effects; most primary epidemiological data are others'.

Hypotheses are often marked (may; a proposed model), but the explanation of the higher recent CUD figure by potency and legal change is offered without data, the cognitive-reversal inference is drawn from a study that did not measure cognition, and the Outlook's statements about industry lobbying carry no citation.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the effects of legal commercial supply
domains.note: The body reports mostly null trend data (stable adult CUD prevalence 2002–2014; no rise in youth use after legalization in the study cited; no overall rise in school-age prevalence 2017–2019) beside rising frequency of use and potency, but the abstract and Outlook present an expected increase in CUD by analogy with alcohol: the evidence of no detectable change is under-represented where readers look first.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used and the overall judgment follows the worst domain (no systematic search). The Primer is careful and largely hedged, but its figures are second-hand and its dependence-risk estimates are on incompatible measures that it does not reconcile. Cite it for the DSM-5 and ICD-11 definitions it tabulates and as a pointer to primary studies and systematic reviews; take every number from the primary source with its definition. A claim resting only on this Primer stays at draft and must say its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

key_findings.finding: Scope and definitions: cannabis means plant material or extracts with substantial THC, the compound acting at CB1 receptors to produce the high; products with no or very little THC (CBD products) are not reviewed. CUD is defined in broad terms as not being able to stop using cannabis despite physical or psychological harm (refs 4, 5).
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 1st, 2nd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Use and burden: by United Nations estimates for 2018, 192 million people (3.9% of the world's adults) had used cannabis in the past year, 9.9% of them daily or near daily (ref 1); 22.1 million people met CUD criteria in 2016, 289.7 cases per 100,000 (ref 6, Global Burden of Disease 2016). Past-year prevalence was highest in North America (12.4%), West and Central Africa (12.4%) and Oceania (10.3%), and lower in Asia (1.8%), North Africa (4.3%) and Eastern and Southern Europe (2.4%) (ref 2).
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 1st paragraph; Epidemiology › Prevalence, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Headline risk: the abstract says CUD affects about 10% of the 193 million people who use cannabis worldwide; the introduction says CUD occurs in about 1 in 10 people who use regularly and in as many as one-third of people who use daily (ref 1), and that people with CUD have higher risks of poor mental health, psychoses and bronchitis (ref 10, a WHO report).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Introduction (unheaded), 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The denominator changes from all past-year use (abstract) to regular use (introduction); see reporting issue 2.

key_findings.finding: Dependence risk: in 1992 the lifetime risk of dependence among people who had ever tried cannabis was estimated at 9%, lower than for tobacco (32%), heroin (23%), cocaine (17%) and alcohol (15%) (ref 30, Anthony, Warner & Kessler, 1994); the risk is said to rise to 30–40% among people with a history of daily use (refs 15, 31). More recent nationally representative US data suggest that about 30% of people who use cannabis may develop CUD (ref 32, Hasin et al., 2015), which the authors say may reflect increases in potency, changes in legal status and social acceptance.
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology › Prevalence, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand and on different measures. The 9% is lifetime DSM-III-R dependence among people who had ever used, from the 1990–92 National Comorbidity Survey (9.1%; card sc_anthony_1994). The Primer does not state the diagnostic system, time frame or denominator of the 30% (Hasin et al., 2015, not read in this project). The 30–40% is cited to two reviews (Budney et al., 2019; Coffey & Patton, 2016). The explanation by potency and legal change is offered without data. The pooled estimates of Leung et al. (2020), CUD 22% (18 to 26) and dependence 13% (10 to 15) among people who use (card sc_leung_2020), are not cited.

key_findings.finding: Frequency of use: the risk of progressing to CUD rises with frequency; US adults with CUD use cannabis on average on 6.2 of 10 days over a year (ref 44); 17.0% of people who smoke weekly and 19.0% of those who smoke daily met dependence criteria, and in a longitudinal study almost 1 in 19 (9.7%) of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (ref 45, Cougle et al., 2016). Co-use of tobacco goes with a higher CUD risk, more withdrawal symptoms and lower cessation rates (ref 46).
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology › Consumption patterns, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: 9.7% is about 1 in 10, not 1 in 19 (reporting issue 1); the 19.0% for daily smoking differs from the 30–40% and the one-third given elsewhere in the Primer (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: Trends and legal supply: legalization is too recent for its full effects on dependence to be judged (ref 15). In US household surveys from 1992 to 2015, adults who used reported using more often than in the preceding decade (ref 28), but adult CUD prevalence was relatively stable from 2002 to 2014 (ref 33); there was no increase in use among adolescents and young adults between 2010 and 2016 (ref 34); among school-age youth, national data for 2017–2019 suggest more daily use and vaping but no rise in overall prevalence (ref 35). Legalization has sharply reduced prices and increased sales of high-potency products (the Primer lists edibles, oils, extracts and waxes containing more than 70% THC; ref 36). Box 1: medical use legal in some form in 34 US jurisdictions, recreational use legal in 12 US states since 2012 and in Canada since 2018.
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology › Prevalence, 3rd paragraph; Box 1
key_findings.note: Ref 34 is, by its title, a study of youth in Washington State after legalization (reporting issue 6).

key_findings.finding: Age at onset: the median age at first use across the Americas, Europe, Asia, New Zealand, the Middle East and Africa is 18–19 years (mean 15–16) (refs 37, 38); first use before 16 increases the risk of CUD, the speed of progression to it, other substance use disorders and anxiety disorders (refs 39–41); use before 18 is associated with more car accidents, antisocial behaviour, polysubstance use and early school dropout than no use or later onset (ref 37). Twin studies show genetic influence on earlier onset after accounting for other substance use, conduct disorder, depression and anxiety (ref 42), and common genetic or shared environmental factors contribute to early onset (refs 37, 42, 43).
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology › Age of onset, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: A mean below the median is unusual for ages at onset (reporting issue 8).

key_findings.finding: Psychiatric comorbidity: in an Australian national sample, 7 in 10 people with CUD had another psychiatric disorder, against 4 in 10 people who used cannabis without CUD and 1.5 in 10 people who did not use it (ref 47); in US national surveys past-year CUD was associated with any mood disorder (odds ratio 3.8), anxiety disorder (2.8), PTSD (4.3) and personality disorder (4.8) (ref 44); 40.5% of Australians with past-year CUD had an anxiety disorder, against 20.8% of people who used without CUD and 11.2% of people who did not use (ref 48). Among people treated for or diagnosed with major depressive disorder, 12% had CUD (ref 50); among people with bipolar disorder 24% used cannabis and 20% had CUD (ref 51); among people with schizophrenia 26.6% had current or lifetime CUD, ranging from 36.7% in the UK to 4.5% in regions outside the UK, Australia, Europe and North America (ref 52).
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology › Co-occurring mental health disorders, 1st–2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Cross-sectional associations; the direction of the links is not addressed in this section.

key_findings.finding: Other substance use: in a US national sample, people with past-year CUD were more likely to have an alcohol use disorder (odds ratio 6.0) and any other drug use disorder (9.0) after adjustment for sex, race and sociodemographic and other variables (ref 44); 83.5% of men and 82.9% of women with past-year CUD had another substance use disorder, and 59.4% and 59.5% an alcohol use disorder (ref 54). Typically three in four people in CUD treatment also have another substance use disorder (cited to DSM-5, ref 4); people who use more drug types have more numerous and more severe psychotic symptoms and more severe depression, anxiety and mania (ref 57).
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology › Cannabis and other substance use, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Gateway question: the Primer says epidemiological and animal studies leave open whether cannabis causally raises the use of other drugs or whether the link reflects shared liability or access to other drugs through markets and peers (refs 58, 59). Box 2: adolescent animals given THC are more likely to self-administer heroin and cocaine, less clearly in adults; statistical modelling shows that shared risk factors can explain the associations (ref 312); adjusting for risk factors reduces but does not remove them; in twins discordant for cannabis use, the twin who used was marginally more likely to use other illicit drugs (ref 313).
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology › Cannabis and other substance use, 3rd paragraph; Box 2

key_findings.finding: Diagnosis: DSM-5 replaced DSM-IV cannabis abuse and dependence with one CUD diagnosis, on evidence that their symptoms lie on a single severity dimension; it requires 2 of 11 criteria with marked impairment or distress over 12 months (mild 2–3, moderate 4–5, severe 6 or more; early remission 3–12 months, sustained remission more than 12 months). ICD-11 distinguishes hazardous use, a harmful pattern of use (similar to DSM-IV abuse) and dependence (similar to DSM-IV dependence), with more scope for clinical judgment. A diagnosis usually requires 12 months of impairment, or 1 month in ICD-11 if use has been daily or almost daily.
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Diagnostic systems, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 and its footnotes; Screening and assessment, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Figures based on DSM-III-R or DSM-IV dependence (for example the 9%) are not on the same scale as DSM-5 CUD, which includes milder cases.

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal: DSM-5 cannabis withdrawal requires, within a week of stopping, three or more of: irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep problems; reduced appetite or weight loss; restlessness; low mood; and at least one physical symptom causing severe discomfort; the signs must also cause clinically severe distress or impairment (the Primer's wording; reduced use is not mentioned). Many of these symptoms also occur in other substance withdrawal or in other mental disorders. Symptoms typically begin 24–48 hours after stopping, peak within the first week and last 1–2 weeks (ref 176). In a US national sample, 12% of people who used frequently had DSM-5 withdrawal in the past 12 months (ref 177); the prevalence among people who use cannabis in the general population is put at 12–17%, and 54% of outpatients and 87% of inpatients with CUD seeking treatment report clinically severe withdrawal (refs 177, 203). Without medical or psychiatric comorbidity, withdrawal is said to pose no serious risk, with most people needing only supportive care, in a sentence that cites no source.
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Diagnostic systems, 3rd paragraph; Management › Cannabis withdrawal, 1st–2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The 12% and the 12–17% refer to different groups (people who use frequently; people who use, in the general population). Ref 203 (Bahji et al., 2020) is read in this round; take its pooled figures from that card. The Primer relabels them (reporting issue 11): by ref 203's title its samples are people with regular or dependent use, and nothing shows that its outcome was restricted to clinically severe withdrawal.

key_findings.finding: Assessment tools: the five-item Severity of Dependence Scale distinguished people who used regularly with and without DSM-III-R dependence with sensitivity 64% and specificity 82% (ref 183); the Timeline Follow-Back agreed with biological markers about 90% of the time (ref 184); both may be unreliable when people have reasons to under-report. In emergency departments, a single question on how often cannabis was used in the past year performed as well as multi-item measures (ref 180).
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Screening and assessment, 2nd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Reward system: THC is thought to raise dopamine activity indirectly, through CB1 receptors on GABA neurons in the ventral tegmental area; THC significantly raised dopamine release in the limbic striatum in two small human PET studies (ref 79), much less than psychostimulants do and more like alcohol (ref 80). Most rodent studies found no conditioned place preference for THC; rats do not reliably self-administer THC, and squirrel monkeys are the only species tested that reliably do (refs 83, 85).
key_findings.locator: Mechanisms/pathophysiology › Endocannabinoids and the reward system, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Murray et al. (2016) describe the same source (Bossong et al., 2015) as one positive and one null PET study with a small but significant increase on combined re-analysis (card sc_murray_2016).

key_findings.finding: Brain alterations, as cited: CB1 receptors are down-regulated in people with CUD, in some studies more with longer duration of smoking, and density normalizes within a few days to 4 weeks of abstinence (refs 94, 98, 99; Figure 4 legend: lower CB1 distribution volume in 30 people who smoked cannabis daily than in 28 controls). Most PET studies found no lower striatal D2/D3 receptor availability (refs 104–107); dopamine release after an amphetamine challenge was lower in people with chronic use (refs 107, 110), perhaps not with mild to moderate dependence (ref 111); dopamine transporter availability was lower in several regions (ref 112); whether these changes reflect vulnerability or neuroadaptation is unclear. A meta-analysis of functional imaging found more striatal and less anterior cingulate and dorsolateral prefrontal activation (ref 114); a structural meta-analysis found smaller hippocampal, orbitofrontal and lateral cortex volumes, with large overlap between groups (ref 116); anatomical effects are judged more modest than those of regular alcohol use (ref 118).
key_findings.locator: Mechanisms/pathophysiology › Brain alterations, 1st–4th paragraphs; Figure 4 legend

key_findings.finding: Cognition: acute and chronic use is associated with poorer performance in several domains in adults, young adults and adolescents (refs 119, 120); acute intoxication affects psychomotor function most, and also short-term memory, attention and inhibition (ref 121). A meta-analysis reported a small but statistically significant correlation of chronic use with cognitive (not motor) impulsivity, cognitive flexibility, attention, and short- and long-term memory (ref 119, Figueiredo et al., 2020). There is some evidence of improvement after sustained abstinence, particularly in learning and memory (ref 121, Broyd et al., 2016), but those studies rarely followed people beyond 4 weeks, and well-controlled longer studies are needed.
key_findings.locator: Mechanisms/pathophysiology › Brain alterations, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: No effect sizes, exposure definitions or abstinence periods are given.

key_findings.finding: Quality of life: heavier use goes with poorer quality of life in a dose–response way (ref 227), and people with CUD report poorer quality of life (refs 228–230); whether it improves after treatment or stopping is uncertain (refs 229, 231, 232). A study of monozygotic twins in which one had never used cannabis and the other had formerly used it heavily found no differences in educational attainment, employment, physical or mental health or health-related quality of life (ref 233), which the authors take as a sign that sustained abstinence may reverse cannabis-related cognitive harm.
key_findings.locator: Quality of life, 2nd–3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: By its title, the twin study (Eisen et al., 2002) measured self-reported health, socio-demographics and quality of life in men, not cognition; the cognitive inference does not follow from it.

key_findings.finding: Other adverse effects, as cited: acute anxiety, depression, and psychotic, cardiovascular and gastrointestinal symptoms (ref 10); dose-related cognitive and psychomotor impairment during intoxication (refs 10, 234–236); a small contribution of cannabis use to motor vehicle crashes (ref 237, Rogeberg & Elvik, 2016); chronic bronchitis reliably associated with regular smoking after controlling for tobacco smoking (ref 10); case series suggesting that heavy smoking can cause hyperemesis syndrome (refs 188, 238) and increase the risk of myocardial infarction and stroke in predisposed people (ref 10); and some epidemiological evidence that fetal growth and development may be harmed by use in pregnancy (ref 10). The major adverse physical effect of smoking cannabis is said to be on the respiratory system (refs 191–193).
key_findings.locator: Quality of life, 4th paragraph; Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Differential diagnosis, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Repeated vomiting: cannabis hyperemesis syndrome has been reported in emergency department patients with cyclical vomiting and current or recent use (ref 188, by its title a case series of 98 patients); its distinction from other cyclical vomiting disorders is underdeveloped, almost all patients with the syndrome use cannabis heavily every week, and 90% report that hot baths and stopping cannabis relieve their symptoms (refs 189, 190).
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Differential diagnosis, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Of the two sources for the 90%, ref 189 is a 2019 clinical review in the BMJ (Chocron, Zuber & Vaucher) and ref 190 is Sorensen et al. (2017), read in this round (card sc_sorensen_2017), so the figure is not independent of that review; it also merges two features that Sorensen et al. report separately (relief with hot bathing; resolution after stopping).

key_findings.finding: Psychosis: the Primer states that psychosis risk rises with the amount of cannabis used and that use worsens schizophrenia symptoms (ref 185); the causal case is contested because the association may result from shared environmental and genetic risk for both CUD and schizophrenia (ref 186, Ksir & Hart, 2016). Cannabis-induced psychosis is a difficult differential diagnosis whose central feature is new psychotic symptoms following cannabis use; patients with substance-induced psychosis typically have more insight, less family history of psychosis, fewer positive and negative symptoms and more severe depression and anxiety than people who use cannabis and have a primary psychotic disorder (ref 187). In the Outlook, a major concern is that high-potency cannabis may increase the risk of psychotic disorders (ref 247, Di Forti et al., 2019).
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Differential diagnosis, 2nd paragraph; Outlook › Potential risks of high-potency products, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: No estimate of psychosis risk is given; the dose–response statement carries a single citation (ref 185). About one in four people with schizophrenia (26.6%) have current or lifetime CUD (ref 52, Epidemiology section).

key_findings.finding: Genetics: a meta-analysis of twin studies attributes 40% (women) and 48% (men) of the variation in starting use, and 59% and 51% of the variation in use with abuse or dependence symptoms, to genetic factors (ref 43, Verweij et al., 2010); in 3,303 Australian twins the heritable influences on cannabis abuse and dependence overlapped largely with those on opportunity and frequency of use (ref 123). Genome-wide studies of cannabis dependence have not found reliable risk alleles; a meta-analysis described as combining eight GWAS is cited for common variants associated with lifetime use accounting for 11% of the variance (ref 129). The Outlook adds that the largest GWAS have not identified loci significantly associated with lifetime use or dependence and that single variants typically explain less than 1% of the variance in CUD risk.
key_findings.locator: Mechanisms/pathophysiology › Aetiology › Genetics, 1st–2nd paragraphs; Outlook › Mechanisms of CUD, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Card sc_pasman_2018 records the 11% as the SNP heritability of lifetime use from all measured variants, with eight independent genome-wide significant variants from three data sources; its cannabis instruments explained 0.15% to 1.12% of the variance. The two passages of the Primer contradict each other (reporting issues 4 and 5).

key_findings.finding: Psychosocial treatment: a meta-analysis of CBT, MET, relapse prevention and contingency management found a moderate pooled effect against control conditions (waiting list, psychological placebo or treatment as usual), Hedges g 0.44 at 2–14 weeks, not differing between DSM-IV abuse and dependence (ref 210); an earlier meta-analysis found Cohen's d 0.81 (ref 211). Combined MET and CBT reduced frequency of use by 25% and doubled abstinence rates against non-active treatment at a median of 4 months; MET and CBT did not differ at 6 months; few interventions maintained gains beyond 9 months (ref 155, Gates et al., 2016, a Cochrane review); very brief interventions (two or fewer sessions, or 60 minutes or less) did not significantly reduce frequency of use or dependence severity (ref 221). The authors judge face-to-face CBT with MET, more than four sessions over more than a month and preferably with contingency management, the most effective treatment for adults; Table 2 rates CBT, MET and their combination medium in effectiveness with moderate-to-high confidence, and contingency management medium as an adjunct.
key_findings.locator: Management › Psychosocial treatments, 2nd–4th paragraphs; Table 2 and its footnotes
key_findings.note: Table 2's confidence ratings are taken from refs 155, 210 and 215 without a stated grading method.

key_findings.finding: Pharmacotherapy: no medication is approved for CUD. A Cochrane review (ref 225) and other reviews found little support for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, bupropion, buspirone or atomoxetine; agonist (THC substitution) and antagonist treatments have shown some short-term reductions in use, but in few, small and poor-quality studies. CB1 agonists such as dronabinol or nabiximols appear to reduce withdrawal severity; in the trials summarized in Table 3, dronabinol improved retention and withdrawal but not abstinence, and nabiximols reduced withdrawal and craving in an inpatient study without a difference in long-term use, and lowered use without better abstinence than placebo in an outpatient pilot. Table 3 lists agents recommended for further research, most tested in single small trials.
key_findings.locator: Management › Pharmacotherapy, 1st paragraph; Management › Cannabis withdrawal, 3rd paragraph; Outlook › Pharmacotherapy, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Prevention: for alcohol and tobacco the most effective approaches reduce supply (price, taxation, minimum purchase age) and restrict advertising, and the authors expect the same to hold where cannabis is legal; evidence that media campaigns reduce drug use is conflicting (refs 16, 17). In a review of primary prevention trials with cannabis-specific content, half of the programmes reported significant but modest effects (median Cohen's d 0.12, against 0.30 for general drug-prevention programmes), and the studies had generally weak methods (ref 196); community-based interventions had limited or no effect on 12-month use (ref 20). Canadian lower-risk cannabis use guidelines (ref 200), endorsed in 2017, are summarized in Box 4 as ten recommendations, which are not extracted on this card.
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Prevention, 1st–2nd paragraphs; Lower-risk cannabis use, 1st paragraph; Box 4

key_findings.finding: Exposure measurement: a major limitation of epidemiological research is that the amount of THC consumed is not adequately measured; usually only frequency is assessed, which hampers the study of risks, of the effects of policy change and of treatment outcomes (refs 249–251); a standard THC unit has been recommended (refs 252, 253), but the variety of products, changing methods of use and the lack of practical measurement technology are obstacles.
key_findings.locator: Outlook › Cannabis consumption measures, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Outlook: legal commercial markets in the USA and Canada may take more than a decade to mature, and their effects on CUD may not be fully assessable until the 2030s; by analogy with alcohol, commercialization is expected to increase the frequency of use among people who already use, through accessibility, acceptability and cheaper high-potency products, with indications that this may be happening (refs 28, 29). People who use high-potency extracts report more dependence symptoms and mental distress than people who use herbal cannabis (ref 245), and in the Netherlands help-seeking to quit rose as potency rose and fell when it declined (ref 246).
key_findings.locator: Outlook › Future effects of legal cannabis, 1st–2nd paragraphs; Outlook › Potential risks of high-potency products, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The statements in the same section about industry lobbying (against taxes and potency caps, for vaping lounges and home delivery) carry no citation.

reporting_issues.issue: Almost 1 in 19 is given as 9.7% for the proportion of people smoking weekly without dependence who became dependent within a year; 9.7% is about 1 in 10 and 1 in 19 is about 5.3% (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Epidemiology › Consumption patterns, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two numbers is wrong; take the transition figure from the primary study (Cougle et al., 2016).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says CUD affects about 10% of 193 million people who use worldwide; the introduction gives 192 million (UN, 2018) and 1 in 10 people who use regularly, and cites a separate estimate of 22.1 million people with CUD in 2016, against about 19 million implied by the abstract (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Abstract; Introduction (unheaded), 1st–2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline figure mixes denominators (all past-year use, regular use) and does not match the burden estimate the Primer cites; it should not be quoted as the risk among all people who use.

reporting_issues.issue: The Primer gives three different dependence risks for daily use (as many as one-third, ref 1; 30–40%, refs 15 and 31; 19.0% of people who smoke daily, ref 45) and two withdrawal prevalences for different groups (12% of people who use frequently; 12–17% of people who use in the general population), without reconciling them.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Introduction (unheaded), 2nd paragraph; Epidemiology › Prevalence, 2nd paragraph; Consumption patterns, 1st paragraph; Diagnostic systems, 3rd paragraph; Management › Cannabis withdrawal, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures rest on different designs and definitions; Leung et al. (2020) show the same split, with dependence among people using weekly or daily of 33% in cohorts and 18% in cross-sectional studies (card sc_leung_2020). Claims must state the source and definition of each figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The genetics passages contradict each other: the Aetiology section cites a meta-analysis of genome-wide studies (ref 129, whose title reports new risk loci for lifetime use) for 11% of the variance, while the Outlook says the largest genome-wide studies have not identified loci significantly associated with lifetime use or dependence, citing among others a study whose title reports a novel locus for cannabis dependence (ref 263).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Mechanisms/pathophysiology › Aetiology › Genetics, 2nd paragraph; Outlook › Mechanisms of CUD, 2nd paragraph; references 129 and 263
reporting_issues.consequence: Genetic statements should be taken from the primary studies, not from either passage.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref 129 (Pasman et al., 2018) is described as a meta-analysis of eight GWAS in which several common variants accounted for 11% of the variance; card sc_pasman_2018 records three data sources (one a consortium of 16 cohorts), eight independent genome-wide significant variants, and 11% as the SNP heritability from all measured variants, with the identified instruments explaining 0.15% to 1.12% of the variance.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Mechanisms/pathophysiology › Aetiology › Genetics, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The 11% is not the variance explained by identified variants; claims on heritability or genetic prediction should cite the Pasman card.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that adolescent and young-adult use did not rise between 2010 and 2016 is cited to ref 34, whose title describes youth in Washington State after legalization.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Epidemiology › Prevalence, 3rd paragraph; reference 34
reporting_issues.consequence: A single-state finding is stated without its setting.

reporting_issues.issue: That three in four people in CUD treatment also have another substance use disorder is cited to the DSM-5 manual (ref 4) rather than to a study.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Epidemiology › Cannabis and other substance use, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: No primary source for the figure.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1, DSM-5 criterion 11 for cannabis use disorder reads as withdrawal syndrome or drinking to prevent withdrawal, wording carried over from alcohol.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Diagnostic systems › Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error in a diagnostic table; quote criteria from DSM-5 itself.

reporting_issues.issue: The median age at first use is given as 18–19 years and the mean as 15–16 years; for ages at onset, which are usually right-skewed, a mean well below the median is unexpected.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Epidemiology › Age of onset, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The two figures may come from different samples or one may be misreported; check refs 37 and 38 before citing either.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference-list errors: ref 120 is printed with pages 461–369 (end before start), ref 246 has no year (its volume and pages, 48, 2346–2352, are printed), and ref 239 prints an author name as Caulk ins.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; identify these sources by DOI or title.

reporting_issues.issue: The Primer relabels Bahji et al.'s pooled withdrawal figures (ref 203): 12–17% becomes the prevalence in the general population of people who use cannabis, and 54% and 87% become the share of outpatients and inpatients with CUD seeking treatment who report clinically severe withdrawal, while ref 203's title describes people with regular or dependent use and nothing in the Primer shows that the outcome was restricted to clinically severe withdrawal. Its account of DSM-5 withdrawal also requires clinically severe distress or impairment and a physical symptom causing severe discomfort, and mentions cessation only.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Diagnostic systems, 3rd paragraph; Management › Cannabis withdrawal, 1st paragraph; reference 203
reporting_issues.consequence: Take withdrawal prevalence from Bahji et al. (card sc_bahji_2020) with that review's own populations and outcome; do not cite the Primer for clinically severe withdrawal or for the wording of the DSM-5 criteria.
